notes.summary: For the exact full envelope, a nonempty family gives a finite lsc raw supremum whose usc defect is an F-sigma meagre discontinuity set. Scalar defect height is bounded by that base defect; this proves no analytic removability or normal sufficiency.
notes.detailedSummary: All real-PL/LFS competitors are continuous at the actual GJR signatures. For every usc obstacle, either the globally real-valued family is empty and both envelopes are minus infinity, or a fixed competitor supplies a continuous baseline. In the latter case s is finite lsc and u=s* is finite usc, h0<=s<=u<=f. The sets {s<=a} intersect {u>=b}, for rational a<b, are closed nowhere dense and cover {s<u}. This defect is exactly the discontinuity set of s. For any continuous surjection q, v=(s composed with q)* satisfies s composed with q<=v<=u composed with q, with finite scalar gap bounded by u-s at the projected point. A closed projection with compact fibers has u(x)=max over the fiber of v. No equality with a newly extended competitor envelope, subharmonicity, small closed defect support or sharp geometric classification follows.
notes.text:
Let U be a good separated strict analytic domain over a complete nontrivially valued field, f:U->R union {-infinity} usc, and E={h:U->R: h<=f and h is locally Fubini--Study or semipositive real PL}, literally the full competitor union. Define s=sup E and u(x)=inf over ordinary open N containing x of sup_N s. GJR Definition 5.1 makes real PL finite continuous; Definition 7.8 makes LFS a real-PL function with semiample residue. Thus both branches are continuous; no maxima closure, invariance, modulus or restricted competitor hypothesis is used. These definitions are retained with exact primary versions. Semiample implies nef, so the union can also be described as the full semipositive real-PL minorant family at these signatures.

If E is empty, s=u=-infinity everywhere under the stipulated extended convention. In particular f=-infinity at even one point forces E empty because every h is globally real-valued. In the nonempty case fix h0 in E. Since f has no +infinity values and is usc, it is locally bounded above. Consequently h0<=s<=u<=f and s,u are finite. For u<=f, given epsilon>0 take an ordinary neighborhood on which f<f(x)+epsilon; the defining infimum gives u(x)<=f(x)+epsilon. The supremum s is lsc since {s>t} is the union over h of the open sets {h>t}.

For rationals a<b define A_ab={s<=a} intersect {u>=b}. It is closed by the two semicontinuities. It has empty interior: if a nonempty open W were contained in A_ab, s<=a on W would give u<=a at every point of W by the neighborhood formula, contradicting u>=b. It is therefore nowhere dense. Every strict finite gap contains rationals s(x)<a<b<u(x), and membership in A_ab forces a strict gap, proving {s<u}=union_{a<b in Q} A_ab. If s is continuous at x then u(x)=s(x). Conversely equality gives, for each epsilon, a local upper bound s<s(x)+epsilon from u and a local lower bound s>s(x)-epsilon from lsc; hence continuity. Thus this defect is exactly the discontinuity set, is F-sigma and meagre. Local compactness and Hausdorffness make U Baire, so its complement is dense G-delta. Relative-boundary points are included. The closure of the defect need not be smaller than U.

For any continuous surjection q:Y->U put v=(s composed with q)*. Regularization majorizes the raw function, and pulling back a base neighborhood gives v(y)<=u(q(y)). The pulled continuous h0 and local upper bound ensure v finite. Therefore 0<=u(q(y))-v(y)<=u(q(y))-s(q(y)), so the strict scalar defect lies over {s<u}, and equality holds on every complete fiber over a continuity point of s.

If q is also closed with compact nonempty fibers, v has a finite maximum m on q^{-1}(x). We have m<=u(x). If m<u(x), choose m<t<u(x). For every y in the fiber, v(y)<t gives an open N_y on which s composed with q<t. A finite union N covers the compact fiber. Closedness of q gives the base neighborhood W=U minus q(Y minus N); its full inverse image lies in N. Surjectivity gives s<t on W, hence u(x)<=t, a contradiction. Thus u(x)=max_{q(y)=x}v(y). This is a proof under explicit topological hypotheses, not a granted scalar theorem.

For a scalar map this comparison concerns the pulled ground-field raw family only. The full freshly defined competitor family upstairs may be larger. A meagre defect can have full closure, and its preimage under a nonopen projection can have interior. No analytic removability, scalar fiber constancy, curvewise positivity, CLD conclusion, continuity conclusion, or normal/geometrically-unibranch classification is proved. This is a continuum topological proof, not a finite computational observation.

The proofs are in argument.md Sections 1-3 and in the self-contained P03.1-paper.tex. Exact versions and complete retained PDFs are listed in input-bindings.json; relevant definitions are in source-extracts/GJR-PL.txt and source-extracts/GJR-pullback-and-LFS.txt. Rerun the owned preparation and build with python prepare_evidence.py and python build_artifacts.py from this directory. No supplied executable is used.

notes.summary: A bounded continuous-family supremum on a real interval has dense meagre defect; a compact proper surjection with connected fibers and a continuous section turns it into an open upstairs defect. This is a topological diagnostic, not an analytic P03.1 counterexample.
notes.detailedSummary: Enumerate rational q_n in [0,1], set s(q_n)=-1/n and s=0 at irrationals. Then s is lsc, s*=0, and s is the increasing supremum of continuous Lipschitz inf-convolutions b_m. Attach a hair of height 1/n at each q_n and project this compact hairy interval to [0,1]. Fibers are compact connected, projection is proper closed surjective, and the continuous base section is a point of local openness. Upstairs regularization is zero on the section and -1/n at positive height on the nth hair. The scalar defect is the nonempty open complement of the base. A continuous idempotent retraction realizes the fiber maximum but does not imply fiber constancy. None of these functions or spaces is asserted analytic or psh.
notes.text:
This sharpness diagnostic complements n1; its construction and calculations are proved here independently. Let q_1,q_2,... enumerate distinct rationals in X=[0,1], ordered by increasing reduced denominator and then numerator, starting with 0 and 1. Define s(q_n)=-1/n and s=0 at irrationals. For every t<0 the set {s<=t} is finite or empty, and for t>=0 it is all of X. Thus s is lsc. Density of irrationals gives s*=0. Its strict defect is exactly the countable dense rational set; the closure of that meagre set is all of X.

For integer m>=1 put b_m(x)=inf_{t in X}(s(t)+m|x-t|). A common Lipschitz bound passes to an infimum, so each b_m is continuous and m-Lipschitz. We have -1<=b_m<=s<=0, and b_m increases with m. Given x and epsilon>0, lsc supplies delta>0 with s(t)>s(x)-epsilon when |t-x|<delta. Outside that radius, s(t)+m|x-t|>=-1+m delta, eventually at least s(x)-epsilon. This proves b_m(x)->s(x). Hence s is a nonempty bounded continuous-family supremum, with no discrete finite surrogate used to prove the claim.

Let Y=(X times {0}) union the hairs {q_n} times [0,1/n], and let q(x,t)=x. Y is closed in the compact square: sequences with unbounded indices have heights tending to zero, while a positive limiting height restricts to finitely many hairs. Thus Y is compact Hausdorff, q is continuous closed surjective and proper, and every fiber is connected (a singleton or an interval). The section sigma(x)=(x,0) is continuous. Every neighborhood of a section point contains nearby base points, so its projected image contains a base neighborhood; projection is open at section points in this precise neighborhood sense.

At (q_n,t) with t>0, there is a neighborhood meeting only the nth hair. Indeed hairs of index sufficiently large have height<t/2; avoid the finitely many other remaining horizontal coordinates and the base. On that neighborhood s composed with q=-1/n. Hence v=(s composed with q)*=-1/n there. At every base point, neighborhoods contain base points of irrational coordinate and v=0. Therefore v(x,0)=0 and v(q_n,t)=-1/n for t>0, whereas s* composed with q=0 everywhere. The strict defect is precisely Y minus (X times {0}), a nonempty open subset of Y. Its image is the meagre rational defect downstairs.

The fiber maximum equals zero and is attained by the section. The continuous idempotent map r=sigma composed with q obeys v composed with r=s* composed with q=0, but v is not constant on any rational fiber. Thus compact connected fibers, a continuous section, openness at the section, the fiber-maximum formula and continuous retraction topology cannot alone force the needed scalar compatibility. This example is consistent with the bounds in n1.

The competitors b_m have not been proved analytic psh, LFS or real PL; Y has not been realized as a scalar-extension analytic space. Consequently this is not a counterexample in the residual normal/geometrically-unibranch scope, and no subharmonicity or nonremovability theorem is inferred from it. It is a mathematical continuum example, not an exhaustive finite result. Its full proof is in argument.md Section 3a and P03.1-paper.tex. Rebuild with python build_artifacts.py and regenerate notes with python make_notes.py. All programs are owned standard-library programs.

notes.text:
Original-scope decision: incomplete, candidate=false. Classical psh means tests on analytic curves after EVERY complete analytic extension; no general theorem here proves them for s* on arbitrary normal higher-dimensional affinoids or arbitrary geometrically unibranch domains. n1 bounds the defect but does not remove it, and n2 proves why a topological continuous-section inference is insufficient. Neither a meagre defect nor a dense defect-free G-delta set supplies analytic removability. No substantive sharp geometric classification has been obtained.

The self-contained paper reconstructs the required necessity phenomena with actual full-family upper bounds and rational LFS lower witnesses. The split branch example uses K<x,y>/(xy) and a positive nodal value restored from one branch; its zero-axis products show the obstruction in higher dimension. The pinched bidisc algebra {g in K<T,Z>:g(0,0)=g(1,0)} is constructed as a bounded strict quotient, with finite normalization, a height-two rational point, and an explicit usc obstacle whose full envelope restores a spike on the other normalization branch. The proof covers affine-algebra seminormality and does not silently assert a freshly verified analytic-stalk comparison. The Q3 nonsplit-node/open-disc surface has a global continuous obstacle and explicit integral-binomial log-max witnesses; a genuine Q3(sqrt(2)) disc test gives a Shilov-boundary contradiction. These are reconstructions of supplied data outside the residual everywhere-geometrically-unibranch class, not new normal counterexamples or new complete classifications. All geometry, formulas and upper/lower bounds are given in argument.md Sections 4-6, with backgrounds and limitations in source-application-ledger.md.

Failed analytic approach: finite maxima of competitors are classically psh, but their directed pointwise limit is the raw s. GR1 Theorem 6.5, whose actual immediate statement and proof were read, proves positivity only if that actual limit is already usc. It cannot insert regularization at points with s<u. Maxima are not assumed real PL with irrational walls. The supplied graph-tube body was inspected as DATA only; after an extension it controls (s composed with pi)*, while the requested tests use s* composed with pi. No equality, analytic section, scalar orbit presentation, finite-flat scalar presentation, globalization cofinality, or subharmonicity-preserving retraction has been proved. A continuous retraction is not asserted analytic. Relative boundary and the empty-family minus-infinity convention are preserved. P03.2 and P03.3 are separate and remain unclaimed.
